_comment: The claims the smoke scenarios prove (#1055). A claim is a short promise with one number, stable forever; its title is at most
ten words (#1817) and everything with a step in it is on its page under live/smoke/claims/. Proof is per provider (#1112): each
providers.<name> cell carries a status, a note and a list of proofs. A proof is a scenario that runs on that provider - scenario,
command, minutes, needs_go, needs_emulator, real_service, break_mode, evidence and an optional note - or, when it is some steps of
another claim's scenario on the same provider, proven_by (that claim), command (that scenario's) and a note naming the steps. A
scenario is the proof of one (claim, provider) cell, which its header states: "# CLAIM N (provider) - <title>. ~M min.".
demos lists the scenarios that prove no claim (import, greenfield, full, and the recommended secure configuration since #1817);
they carry no CLAIM header and belong to no cell. live/smoke_claims_test.go holds this file to the scenario directory and to the
per-claim pages, and site/data/claims.json is a byte-for-byte copy the site renders.
status is one of: proven (a proof runs on that provider and its BREAK control catches), restated (the promise holds in a weaker
form, said in note), n/a (the substrate has no such concept), open (no proof yet: a gap, not a shrug).
substrate lists the providers the promise applies to: every cell that is not n/a.
retired lists numbers that are no longer claims of their own. Most were a second proof of an existing promise, filed as a claim; each
now lives in the named claim's cell for that provider, its slug is still its scenario's name, and its number is never reused. #1817
folded 27 of them into the 16 promises left; a retired entry with demo: true is a scenario that is now a demo instead.

real_service: true marks a proof whose scenario cannot run against the emulator honestly and runs against that provider's real account instead. It is maintainer-run (SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1 for aws, the only provider this is proven true for today), never CI-gated, and its cell reads proven from a maintainer's run recorded in the note, not from CI. live/smoke_claims_test.go holds the flag to the scenario's own refusal. The field is per-proof rather than per-provider (#1598), so a second real-account provider sets real_service on its own proof instead of the schema growing a provider-named field.

needs_emulator: true marks a proof whose scenario runs on one substrate and keeps its records on another - today a Kubernetes proof that also brings up the pinned floci emulator for an S3-backed record store, on top of kind and kubectl. An aws proof is never asked to carry it: there the emulator IS the substrate, which the column already says.

Scenario file names may carry a provider-specific prefix for readability (k8s- for a Kubernetes proof); it is a naming convention only, kept because renaming the files would be noisy for no gain. No code may read a scenario's provider, or whether it needs_emulator or is real_service, off that prefix - the provider a scenario proves is always the providers.<name> key that names its cell, never its file name (#1598, #1593).

BREAK=1 sets recovery_window_in_days = 0, which the provider sends as ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery, and requires the opposite outcome - DescribeSecret answering ResourceNotFoundException after the destroy and the replan empty - because without that control the main arm's secret still being there after the destroy would read the same if choudoufu never sent the delete
proofs.note: The AWS form of an accepted, unfinished delete is a scheduled one (#1599): Secrets Manager's DeleteSecret with a recovery window, like KMS's ScheduleKeyDeletion, answers success and leaves the resource in the account, tags included, until the window ends. hashicorp/aws 6.58.0 reads it as gone - findSecretByID returns NotFound once DeletedDate is set, findKeyByID once KeyState is PendingDeletion, and each delete waits on exactly that - so the half of this promise that holds on AWS is the second: the plan after the delete is empty, as stock's is, with no second destroy (which AWS would refuse for the whole window) and no refusal of the swept, still-marked object. The first half, an object the provider still reads as present after its own delete returned, needs an eventually consistent delete; the pinned emulator does not model that lag (lex00/floci#216), and most hashicorp/aws deletes wait it out. This proof was claim 25 on AWS, which read restated: it measures the second half of a held delete, the plan after it, and not the first.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 strips the label from the orphan and requires the replan to leave it alone; the ordinary run strips the orphan's address annotation first and requires it to be proposed all the same

BREAK=1 removes the finalizer before the destroying apply and requires the opposite outcome - the object gone in one apply and the replan empty - because without that control the scenario would read identically if choudoufu simply never deleted a ConfigMap

BREAK=1 runs the identical namespace delete and then asserts what a sweep that never saw it would plan, "No changes.", over the real plan; that assertion must fail, and the control passes only when the plan instead proposes the three creates, because without it the creates of step 4 would read the same if the plan proposed them whatever the cluster held
proofs.note: A namespace deleted under a converged estate takes its objects with it, and the plan reads them as gone: nothing in it is listed or swept as an orphan, and the plan is the one stock's plan makes from the same position, measured on the same cluster rather than quoted. Step 7, a deleted record-store namespace, is claim 29's (#1765).

kubernetes.note: The sweep is one cluster-wide, label-selected list per kind rather than one account-wide call, and controller-made objects (owner references, or written only by the control plane) are excluded before anything reaches a delete. An object no natural key declares is joined a second way, by the block its address annotation names (#1640): bound when that block is declared, an orphan otherwise. The label is what makes an object this estate's, so an orphan whose annotation was stripped is still proposed for removal; two objects whose annotations claim one block that holds neither are refused as a collision rather than both destroyed (#1641).

Steps 3 and 10 of claim 29's Kubernetes scenario (#1392, #1441). Step 3 kills an apply with SIGKILL mid-flight and the very next run carries on, with nothing in the records namespace a Lease or anything else lock-shaped. claims.title: A crash is fixed by re-running

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 strips the ownership markers off everything the killed apply created, leaving the same objects in the same account with no ownership on them; the re-run must then be unable to bind and must build a duplicate VPC, which is stock's behaviour, and a strip that left a marker behind fails the control rather than passing it
proofs.note: Scoped to what the dead apply MARKED. An object killed between its create call and the marker write that follows it is not named by the next plan, and for a tag_on_create=false type that window is the whole of the provider's create step: 15.0s for a hosted zone against the pinned emulator. The re-run then duplicates it and the orphan is removed by hand. Ten types read tag_on_create false in live/registry.json (#1084); for every other type the markers ride the create call and the window does not exist. A record-carried instance's effect is at-least-once: the record is written after the whole walk, so a killed run leaves an effect that ran and no record of it, and the next plan names it as a create. Step 7 then deletes every local file - the cache, the lock file, the whole .terraform directory - and the next plan from a fresh init is still empty (claim 5's original proof, moved here by #1817).

kubernetes.note: An apply SIGKILLed between one ConfigMap's create and the next leaves one labelled object and no record of either; the next plan binds the created object by its label, namespace and name, proposes only what was never reached, and the re-run keeps that object's uid and replans empty. The property is also measured by live/GAUNTLET.md stage 10 (day2_crash) on every kind-lane estate.

A carve is one label write, tofu-estate=<new> on the object, through live-mv -from-estate or kubectl label; with the admission policy installed the caller must hold both estates, and claim 13's Kubernetes scenario (k8s-the-label-is-the-boundary) measures the refusal without the grant and the carve with it (#1081, item 5).

Any kubectl reads both. The sweep binds an object no natural key declares to the block its annotation names (#1640), so a block whose name is read at plan time applies and replans empty, and a create_before_destroy rename plans as the replace stock plans (#1541, #1641). A rename rewrites the annotation (a moved block plans it, live-mv writes it); a move between estates is the one label write live-mv -from-estate makes under the caller's credential, judged by the admission policy (claim 13 on Kubernetes). A count pool's fungible set, the AWS proof count-is-a-fungible-set, does not arise here: the API server keeps names unique per kind and namespace, so a count-expanded set carries distinct names and no slot is written.

Steps 2, 4, 5 and 9 of claim 29's Kubernetes scenario (#1392). Step 2: a Kubernetes-only estate's first apply writes its first record as a Secret, with no AWS credentials in the environment, and the replan reads it back. Step 4: a role scoped to one records namespace cannot read another estate's records, and a role given list and get on a shared namespace reads every estate in it, which is the bargain: the namespace is the boundary, all or nothing. Step 5: every record Secret carries tofu-estate, so the estate-boundary admission policy refuses a write by another estate's identity with no policy added for the store. Step 9: an identity holding get and list on the record Secrets plans and writes nothing, and is refused the apply naming create, update and delete. BREAK=1 widens the plan role to cluster-wide secret reads and removes the admission policy, and requires the other estate's records to be read and the cross-estate write to land.

kubernetes.note: Two estates whose key_prefix values prefix one another, the hazard the AWS name-prefix proof measures, are not measured here: KubernetesStore names each record Secret by a SHA-256 of its whole key and refuses a key-annotation mismatch with KeyCollisionError, so a broken delimiter would produce a collision or a refusal rather than a silent read, and no scenario pins which.

Steps 1, 2, 3, 8 and 9 each have a control that runs the step's own check function against a world built to fail it and requires the failure by name: the suite skipped and the suite short one case, the record Secrets stripped of their annotation and then their label, a planted Lease and a lock-named Secret, the Role short one verb given that verb so the same apply goes through and leaves records behind, and a write between the two resourceVersion dumps and a dump of a namespace holding no record; the listings behind steps 3, 8 and 9 are also run through a kubeconfig that reaches no server and must fail rather than read as empty

claims.title: No secret survives unless you let it

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 applies the same estate under secrets = "store" and runs the identical scan over the identical set of files, which must then find the password (it finds it in the record and the cache); a scan that finds nothing there fails the run, because its zero under refuse would prove nothing
proofs.note: The saved plan (-out) and a TF_LOG=debug file are read separately and do hold the value, as they do on stock. Under refuse the argument is proposed on every plan, rotated or not, and the scenario asserts both arms (#1503).

kubernetes.note: Under strict { secrets = "refuse" } on a kind cluster, a random_password is refused by name with nothing written, a kubernetes_secret_v1 fed from the environment applies with no state cache and the value in no kept file (6 files scanned), and the replan is empty because the API server returns the data; a rotated value is still proposed. The first run (2026-10-04) failed the empty replan on + wait_for_service_account_token, a configuration-only argument refuse used to leave unrecorded on any type holding a secret; since #1873 refuse drops each sensitive argument and records the rest.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 applies the identical estate under secrets = "store" and runs the identical scan, which must find the value (it finds it in the state cache); a scan that finds nothing there fails the run, because its zero under refuse would prove nothing

BREAK=1 renders the consumer's role without --reads-outputs-of network and leaves its configuration declaring the read; the plan must then refuse with "This estate may not read another estate's outputs", naming estate network and the flag, and a plan that shows network's value fails the control
proofs.note: On the pinned emulator with its IAM filter on. The emulator does not evaluate s3:prefix, s3:RequestObjectTag or s3:ExistingObjectTag, so the Allow statements run without their conditions and the tag Denies do not fire; the refusal here comes from the resource scope of the one statement --reads-outputs-of adds. Claim 28's one-bucket-many-estates proof measures the tag-conditioned half on real AWS. Only non-sensitive, wholly known root outputs are recorded, so only those cross.

kubernetes.note: On Kubernetes the declaration is the reader's record_store block: reads_outputs_of "<estate>" {} opens that estate's records namespace through a store that can only get. An undeclared read is refused before anything is sent, under an identity RBAC would have let through; a declared read plans with the producer's value through a grant of one get and says how old it is; after the producer's destroy deletes its recorded output, the consumer is told so by name.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 declares the read and withholds the Role granting get on the producer's output Secret, and requires the plan to refuse naming estate network, its namespace and the Role

BREAK=1 removes the estate's own ignore_tags declaration - the one piece of configuration the claim is about, not a choudoufu code path - and runs the identical out-of-band AWS CLI tag write; it passes only when the plan now proposes an update naming the tag, because choudoufu has no tag-diffing of its own to defeat with a build overlay: a resource's tags are planned entirely by the real hashicorp/aws provider process, the same one a stock run talks to
proofs.note: A tag another account's automation or an AWS service adds out of band does not churn the plan once the estate tells its provider to ignore that key, the same knob stock gives every AWS user, and an edit to a tag the estate does declare still plans (#1624). This is the managed-resource half only: a tag added out of band to a record object choudoufu wrote is not a plan-time question, because S3Store.PutIfVersion replaces an object's whole tag set on every write and no code path diffs a record object's tags against a configured value. Established by reading the store's write path, not by a scenario step.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 runs the identical kubectl command against a key the configuration does NOT declare - same object, same --overwrite, one key different - and requires the opposite outcome, "No changes.", with the label still on the object afterwards. Without it every plan the main arm requires would read the same if choudoufu simply planned on any difference between the configuration and the live object, and step 5's point - that the provider's computed_fields rule still keeps the server's own keys out of the plan - would be scenery. It then runs one control for steps 8 and 9 together: the same two working directories on record_store "local", where the second one has no record to read and must plan "No changes." instead of the removal, which is what a Kubernetes estate on the implied store gives its second operator today.
proofs.note: A key the configuration never declared - the API server's own kubernetes.io/metadata.name, a controller's annotation - stays the server's and churns nothing, with no estate configuration needed, because kubernetes_manifest's computed_fields reads the prior manifest to decide what to keep. A label or annotation edited, added or deleted in the configuration plans the one in-place update stock plans, and a second working directory with no record of its own removes the same label when the estate shares its records.
